category.title: Strings & Pattern Matching
category.description: String manipulation, pattern searching (KMP, Z-algorithm), and hashing.

algorithms.title: KMP Algorithm (Knuth-Morris-Pratt Pattern Matching)
algorithms.summary: Efficiently finds pattern matches in a text string without re-checking matching characters using the Longest Proper Prefix which is also Suffix (LPS) table.
explanation: Precompute the `LPS` (Longest Prefix Suffix) array for the pattern of length M.
`LPS[i]` stores the length of the longest matching proper prefix of `pattern[0...i]` that is also a suffix of `pattern[0...i]`.
Scan the text of length N with index `i` and pattern with index `j`.
When characters match (`text[i] == pattern[j]`), advance both `i++` and `j++`.
When a mismatch occurs, use `LPS[j-1]` to skip redundant pattern comparisons instead of resetting `i` back.

traceSteps: Step 1: Compute LPS array for 'ABACABA' -> LPS = [0, 0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 3].
Step 2: Match text and pattern:
i=0..4: 'ABABA' matches 'ABABA', mismatch at text[5]='C' vs pattern[5]='B'.
Use LPS[4] = 1: shift pattern pointer j to 1. Match resumes.
i=6..12: 'ABACABA' matches pattern 'ABACABA' completely (j = 7 = len(pattern)).
Pattern matched at index 6 in O(N + M) linear time.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds exact occurrences of a pattern P of length M inside text T of length N in linear time.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When searching for substrings in huge text corpora, DNA sequence matching, or avoiding worst-case O(N * M) naive string matching.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Text editor search utilities (`grep`, Ctrl+F), genomic sequence search tools (BLAST), network packet filtering.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Eliminates backtracking in the primary text stream. Time complexity remains linear O(N + M) regardless of text repetitions.

algorithms.title: Rabin-Karp Algorithm (Polynomial Rolling Hash Matching)
algorithms.summary: Uses rolling hash techniques to find pattern matches in linear average time by maintaining a sliding hash value.
explanation: Compute the polynomial hash of the pattern of length M: hash(P) = sum(P[i] * B^(M-1-i)) % MOD.
Compute the initial hash of the first window of text of length M.
Slide the window over the text one character at a time:
- Subtract the outgoing character's contribution: (hash - text[old] * B^(M-1)) % MOD.
- Shift left: (hash * B) % MOD.
- Add the incoming character's contribution: (hash + text[new]) % MOD.
If the text window hash equals the pattern hash, perform a character-by-character comparison to handle hash collisions.

exampleTrace.input: text = 'GEEKS FOR GEEKS', pattern = 'GEEK', prime q = 101
exampleTrace.output: Pattern found at index 0 and index 10
traceSteps: Step 1: Calculate hash for pattern 'GEEK' = H_p.
Step 2: Calculate hash for first window text[0..3] 'GEEK' = H_w.
Step 3: Window 0: H_w == H_p. Character-by-character check matches 'GEEK' at index 0.
Step 4: Roll hash for window 1 text[1..4] 'EEKS': subtract 'G', multiply base, add 'S' mod 101.
Step 5: Continue rolling window hash until window 10 text[10..13] 'GEEK': H_w == H_p. Match at index 10.
Pattern matches found in O(N + M) average time.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds pattern occurrences in text and handles multiple pattern search efficiently using rolling hashes.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When searching for multiple patterns simultaneously, detecting duplicate substrings, or checking plagiarism.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Plagiarism detectors, virus signature scanning in antivirus software, DNA motif matching.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Recomputes substring hash in O(1) time per step instead of re-hashing from scratch O(M).

algorithms.title: Z-Algorithm (Linear Time Z-Array Pattern Search)
algorithms.summary: Constructs a Z-array where Z[i] is the length of the longest substring starting at i that matches the prefix of the concatenated string P + '$' + T.
explanation: Construct concatenated string S = pattern + '$' + text.
Maintain a Z-box [L, R] which is the segment of S matching a prefix of S with maximum right endpoint R.
For index i from 1 to len(S):
- If i > R: Compute Z[i] naively by comparing S[i+k] with S[k], then update [L, R] = [i, i + Z[i] - 1].
- If i <= R: Use previously computed Z[i - L]. If Z[i - L] < R - i + 1, then Z[i] = Z[i - L]. Otherwise extend naively beyond R and update [L, R].
Check indices where Z[i] == len(pattern) to find exact match positions.

exampleTrace.output: Z-array computed, Pattern matched where Z[i] == len(pattern)
traceSteps: Construct concatenated string P + '$' + T = 'aab$aabxaaab'.
Maintain Z-box window [L, R] = [0, 0].
i=4 (first 'a' of T): S[4..6]='aab' matches prefix S[0..2]='aab' -> Z[4] = 3 (length of pattern 'aab')!
Since Z[4] == len('aab') == 3, pattern 'aab' is matched at text index 0.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds all occurrences of a pattern in a text in O(N + M) time and finds longest common prefixes.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When needing linear time pattern matching, finding period of a string, or prefix-suffix overlaps.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Bioinformatics DNA sequence alignment, text editor search engines, string compression algorithms.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Reuses previously calculated prefix match bounds [L, R] to process each character in O(1) amortized time.

algorithms.title: Manacher's Algorithm (Longest Palindromic Substring in O(N))
algorithms.summary: Finds the longest palindromic substring in linear time O(N) by transforming the string to handle even/odd lengths and reusing symmetry.
explanation: Transform string S by inserting boundary characters (e.g. 'abc' -> '#a#b#c#').
Maintain an array P[i] representing the radius of the palindrome centered at i.
Maintain center C and right boundary R of the furthest-reaching palindrome.
For index i:
- Find mirror index i_mirror = 2*C - i.
- If i < R, set initial P[i] = min(R - i, P[i_mirror]).
- Expand around i while characters match.
- If palindrome expands past R, update C = i and R = i + P[i].
Find index with maximum P[i] to extract the longest palindrome.

traceSteps: Step 1: Transform string with delimiters: T = '^#b#a#b#a#d#$'.
Step 2: Maintain center C = 0, right boundary R = 0, radius array P.
Step 3: Expand around centers using mirror i_mirror = 2*C - i.
Max radius found at center 3 (corresponding to 'a' in 'bab'): P[3] = 3.
Step 4: Extract longest palindrome substring from original string -> 'bab'.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds the longest palindromic substring in O(N) time instead of O(N^2) or O(N^3).
wAnswers.whenToUse: When finding longest palindrome or counting palindromic substrings in strict linear time bounds.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Genomic DNA palindromic sequence analysis, text processing, data compression.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Reuses palindrome symmetry (mirroring) to avoid re-expanding characters inside known palindromes.

codeTemplates.code:
def longest_palindrome_manacher(s):
    if not s: return ''
    t = '#' + '#'.join(s) + '#'
    n = len(t)
    p = [0] * n
    c = r = 0
    max_len = max_center = 0

    for i in range(n):
        mirror = 2 * c - i
        if i < r:
            p[i] = min(r - i, p[mirror])
        while i + 1 + p[i] < n and i - 1 - p[i] >= 0 and t[i + 1 + p[i]] == t[i - 1 - p[i]]:
            p[i] += 1
        if i + p[i] > r:
            c = i
            r = i + p[i]
        if p[i] > max_len:
            max_len = p[i]
            max_center = i

    start = (max_center - max_len) // 2
    return s[start : start + max_len]

algorithms.title: Expand Around Center (Palindromic Substrings)
algorithms.summary: Iterates over all 2N-1 potential centers (single characters and gaps between adjacent characters) and expands outward to find all palindromes.
explanation: Every palindrome has a center: single character for odd-length (e.g., 'aba'), or gap for even-length (e.g., 'abba').
For each index i from 0 to N-1:
- Call helper expand(left=i, right=i) for odd length palindromes.
- Call helper expand(left=i, right=i+1) for even length palindromes.
In helper: while left >= 0 and right < N and S[left] == S[right], decrement left and increment right.
Track max length found and return the longest palindrome substring.

traceSteps: Odd-length centers (i, i):
Center i=0 ('b'): max len = 1 ('b').
Center i=1 ('a'): expand left (0: 'b') & right (2: 'b') -> 'b' == 'b' -> max len = 3 ('bab').
Center i=2 ('b'): expand left (1: 'a') & right (3: 'a') -> 'a' == 'a' -> max len = 3 ('aba').
Even-length centers (i, i+1): No palindrome > 1.
Longest Palindromic Substring = 'bab'.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds longest palindromic substring or counts total palindromic substrings with O(1) space.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When interviewed on palindrome problems where O(N²) time is optimal enough and O(1) space is preferred over Manacher's complexity.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Interview coding assessments, string validation routines.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Requires 0 extra memory (O(1) auxiliary space) compared to Dynamic Programming (O(N²)) or Manacher's (O(N) memory).

algorithms.title: Minimum Window Substring (Sliding Window & Hash Map)
algorithms.summary: Finds the smallest substring in S that contains all characters of string T (including duplicates) using two pointers and frequency counting.
explanation: Build target frequency map target_counts for string T.
Maintain window frequency map window_counts and two pointers left = 0, right = 0.
Maintain matched_chars count representing characters meeting required frequency in window.
Expand right pointer:
- Add S[right] to window_counts.
- If window_counts[c] == target_counts[c], increment matched_chars.
When matched_chars == len(target_counts) (valid window):
- Update minimum window size and start position.
- Contract window from left pointer to find minimal valid length.

traceSteps: Target freq map: {'A':1, 'B':1, 'C':1}. Required matches = 3.
Expand right pointer r:
r=0 ('A'): match count = 1.
r=3 ('B'): match count = 2.
r=5 ('C'): match count = 3. Window s[0..5] = 'ADOBEC' contains all target chars! Window len = 6.
Shrink left pointer l to minimize window:
Shrink l to 3: s[3..10] 'BECODEBA' valid.
Continue until right pointer reaches index 12 ('C'): Window s[9..12] = 'BANC' has len 4 with all target chars.
Minimum Window Substring = 'BANC'.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Finds smallest window containing all required characters in linear time.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When finding minimal/maximal contiguous substring containing a target set of items.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Search query snippet generation (finding paragraph containing all user search keywords), log analytics.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Both left and right pointers traverse the string at most once, guaranteeing linear O(N) execution.

codeTemplates.code:
from collections import Counter

def min_window(s, t):
    if not s or not t: return ''
    target_counts = Counter(t)
    required = len(target_counts)
    window_counts = {}
    formed = 0
    l = r = 0
    ans = (float('inf'), None, None)

    while r < len(s):
        char = s[r]
        window_counts[char] = window_counts.get(char, 0) + 1
        if char in target_counts and window_counts[char] == target_counts[char]:
            formed += 1
        while l <= r and formed == required:
            char = s[l]
            if r - l + 1 < ans[0]:
                ans = (r - l + 1, l, r)
            window_counts[char] -= 1
            if char in target_counts and window_counts[char] < target_counts[char]:
                formed -= 1
            l += 1
        r += 1
    return '' if ans[0] == float('inf') else s[ans[1]:ans[2]+1]

algorithms.title: String Hashing & Polynomial Rolling Hash (Substrings in O(1))
algorithms.summary: Computes prefix hash array and prime powers so any substring hash S[L...R] can be checked for equality in O(1) time.
explanation: Compute prefix hash array prefix_hash[i] = (prefix_hash[i-1] * P + ord(S[i])) % MOD.
Precompute prime power array P_pow[i] = (P_pow[i-1] * P) % MOD.
To get hash of substring S[L...R] in O(1):
- hash(L, R) = (prefix_hash[R+1] - prefix_hash[L] * P_pow[R - L + 1]) % MOD.
- Handle negative mod results by adding MOD.
Use Double Hashing (two prime moduli e.g. 10^9+7 and 10^9+9) to eliminate collision risk.

traceSteps: Compute prefix hash array H and power array P with base p = 31, mod = 10^9+7.
Query 1: Hash(0, 4) = (H[4] - 0) mod M.
Query 2: Hash(5, 9) = (H[9] - H[4] * P[5]) mod M.
Compare Hash(0, 4) == Hash(5, 9) -> Both evaluate to 3105741.
Substrings s[0..4] and s[5..9] are identical! Answered in O(1) time.

wAnswers.whatItSolves: Allows comparing any two substrings of a string in O(1) time without character-by-character loop.
wAnswers.whenToUse: When problem involves frequent substring equality checks, finding repeated substrings, or Palindrome queries.
wAnswers.whereUsed: Competitive programming string processing, diff tools, duplicate document analysis.
wAnswers.whyOptimal: Reduces substring comparisons from O(K) time to instantaneous O(1) mathematical lookup.
